title: TASS vs. Infectious Endophthalmitis: The Post-Op Crisis
summary: Differentiating Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) from infectious endophthalmitis is the most critical diagnostic challenge in the immediate postoperative period. While TASS is a sterile inflammatory response to an intraocular insult, endophthalmitis is a vision-threatening infection requiring urgent antimicrobial intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS) is an acute, sterile, non-infectious intraocular inflammation caused by a non-infectious substance entering the anterior segment, resulting in toxic damage to intraocular tissues. Acute Endophthalmitis is a severe intraocular infection (usually bacterial) involving the vitreous and aqueous humors, often occurring within 1 week of surgery.

sections.title: The Golden Clock: Time of Onset
content: TASS: 12–24 hours post-op (can occur as early as 6h).
Acute Virulent Endo: 24–48 hours (Streptococcus, Pseudomonas).
Typical Endo: 3–7 days post-op (Staph epidermidis).
Delayed-Onset Endo: Weeks to months (P. acnes, Fungal).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Think Endophthalmitis!
content: Profound, sudden loss of vision (Light Perception or worse)
Severe eye pain and periorbital headache
Marked chemosis and eyelid edema
Presence of vitreous membranes/cells on B-scan
Failure to respond to intensive topical steroids after 6 hours

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Clinical History (Onset time is critical)
Step 2: Slit Lamp (Look for limbus-to-limbus edema vs vitritis)
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasonography (Assess vitreous status)
Step 4: If suspicious for Endo: AC & Vitreous Tap for culture/gram stain
Step 5: PCR Analysis (If available, for rapid pathogen ID)

content.explanation: T: Timeline (Acute <24h); A: Anterior focus (No Vitritis); S: Sterile (Culture Negative); S: Steroid response (Rapid improvement).

sections.title: Management: TASS Protocol
content: Intensive Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1% every 30-60 mins)
Topical NSAIDs as adjunct
Aqueous Suppressants (if IOP > 30 mmHg)
Close follow-up (every 6-12 hours initially)
Rule out infection if no response in 24 hours

sections.title: Management: Endophthalmitis Protocol
content: Intravitreal Vancomycin (1mg/0.1mL) + Ceftazidime (2.25mg/0.1mL)
AC/Vitreous Tap & Gown (Before antibiotics)
Immediate Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) if Vision is Light Perception (LP) or worse
Intensive Topical Fortified Antibiotics (Vancomycin/Tobramycin)
Systemic Antibiotics (Controversial, except in specific cases)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Pearl: EVS Study
content: EVS (Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study) Findings:
Primary outcome: PPV is superior to Tap/Inject ONLY if presenting vision is Light Perception (LP).
If vision is Hand Motion (HM) or better, Tap/Inject is equivalent to PPV.
Systemic antibiotics (Amikacin/Ceftazidime) showed NO benefit for visual outcome.
Diabetes was a significant risk factor for worse outcomes.

sections.title: Prevention Checklist
content: Strict instrument cleaning protocols (No enzymatic detergents)
Single-use cannulas preferred
Minimize volume of intracameral medications
Wait 20 mins after ETO sterilization for off-gassing
Regular autoclave maintenance & biological indicators

content.explanation: TASS often presents with a 'cold' hypopyon—one that shifts easily with head movement and is associated with a white, quiet conjunctiva—whereas infectious endophthalmitis presents with a 'hot' hypopyon, often fibrin-locked and associated with angry, injected conjunctiva/chemosis.
